Google Cloud: exposure and health checks ​

Verified against primary documentation on 2026-10-11.

Exposure ​

Load balancers are external or internal, defined by where the client is: an external load balancer is for clients that "need to reach your application from the internet", an internal one for clients "inside of Google Cloud". Scope (global, regional, cross-region) and layer (Application or Network) are separate axes, so product names combine all three, such as "regional internal Application Load Balancer" (Cloud Load Balancing overview).

Addresses follow the same words. An internal IP "cannot be reached from the internet"; an external IP is "reachable by any host on the internet" (IP addresses). "Private" names connectivity products instead: Private Google Access, Private Service Connect and private services access (Private access options).

Cloud Run ingress takes all, internal or internal-and-cloud-load-balancing. The last one admits internet traffic only through the external Application Load Balancer, so Cloud Armor, IAP and CDN apply to every public request (Restrict network ingress for Cloud Run).

On GKE, a LoadBalancer Service becomes internal with the annotation networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal" (About LoadBalancer Services). Gateway classes carry the same vocabulary: gke-l7-global-external-managed, gke-l7-regional-external-managed, gke-l7-rilb and gke-l7-cross-regional-internal-managed-mc (About Gateway API). The control plane is the exception: it has a private endpoint and an optional public endpoint, which Google advises enabling "only if you require external administrative access" (Private cluster concepts).

One endpoint for gRPC and REST ​

Google's own APIs serve gRPC and REST/JSON on the same host and port, told apart by path. An API service endpoint is "a network address that an API service uses to handle incoming API requests", such as https://pubsub.googleapis.com (API design glossary). Each method is defined once as an RPC, and an HTTP binding on it also presents that method as a REST/JSON resource path (AIP-127: HTTP and gRPC Transcoding). The URLs differ, the endpoint does not:

CallPath on pubsub.googleapis.com:443Answers with
gRPC ListTopicsPOST /google.pubsub.v1.Publisher/ListTopicsapplication/grpc, grpc-status
REST projects.topicsGET /v1/projects/{project}/topicsapplication/json

Observed on 2026-10-12 with unauthenticated requests: the gRPC path answered content-type: application/grpc with a grpc-status trailer, and the REST path answered content-type: application/json, both over HTTP/2 on port 443:

sh
curl -s --http2 -D - -o /dev/null -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/grpc' -H 'te: trailers' \
  https://pubsub.googleapis.com/google.pubsub.v1.Publisher/ListTopics
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null https://pubsub.googleapis.com/v1/projects/x/topics

One port for gRPC and HTTP ​

Application Load Balancers talk to backends over HTTP, HTTPS, HTTP2 or H2C. HTTP2 "uses HTTP/2 and TLS (HTTP/2 without encryption isn't supported.)", while H2C "uses HTTP/2 over TCP. TLS isn't required. H2C isn't supported for classic Application Load Balancers". The load balancer "doesn't fall back to a different protocol" when the backend does not speak the one configured. The gRPC backend protocol exists only for Cloud Service Mesh (Backend services overview), so a load balancer reaches gRPC and other routes on one port through an HTTP2 backend for a TLS port, or an H2C backend for a plaintext one. H2C is also available to load balancers created by the GKE Gateway controller (External Application Load Balancer overview). The rule to "use only gRPC or TCP health checks" applies to backend services whose protocol is gRPC, not to an HTTP2 or H2C backend (Health checks overview). A gRPC health check passes only on status OK with SERVING, and comes in grpc and grpc_with_tls forms.

Identity ​

Network reach and identity are separate settings. On Cloud Run, "IAM authentication still applies to requests reaching the service ... from any of the preceding network ingress paths" (Restrict network ingress for Cloud Run), and public access means granting allUsers the roles/run.invoker role.

Staff tools sit behind Identity-Aware Proxy, which "lets you establish a central authorization layer for applications accessed by HTTPS, so you can use an application-level access control model instead of relying on network-level firewalls" (Identity-Aware Proxy overview).

Health checks ​

GKE Ingress builds its load balancer health check outside the cluster. A BackendConfig on the Service takes precedence; without one, the GKE Ingress controller infers what it can, such as path, port and protocol, from the serving Pods' readinessProbe, and uses defaults for the rest (Troubleshooting Ingress health checks). It reads the probe only when its port "must match the actual port your application is listening on within the container", that containerPort "must match the Service's targetPort", and the Ingress backend references that Service port. A readiness probe on another port, such as private while the Ingress routes to public, leaves the default / check in place, so the health check has to come from a BackendConfig with healthCheck.requestPath and healthCheck.port. GKE Gateway does not: it requests / unless a HealthCheckPolicy says otherwise (Configure Gateway resources).

Health check source ranges depend on the load balancer and backend type. For an external Application Load Balancer with instance group or zonal NEG backends, probes come from 35.191.0.0/16 (2600:2d00:1:b029::/64 for IPv6) and proxied traffic also from 130.211.0.0/22; regional and cross-region load balancers send traffic from their proxy-only subnet instead of 130.211.0.0/22 (Firewall rules for health checks). For backend services that use gRPC, Google says to "use only gRPC or TCP health checks. Don't use HTTP(S) or HTTP/2 health checks" (Health checks overview).

Cloud Run supports startup probes over HTTP, TCP and gRPC, and liveness probes over HTTP and gRPC (Configure container health checks). It reserves paths starting with /_ah/ and "some paths ending with z", and recommends "avoiding all paths that end in z" (Cloud Run known issues).
